title: Of diversion
paragraphs: I was once employed in consoling a lady who was truly afflicted. Most of their mournings are artificial and ceremonious:
"Uberibus semper lacrymis, semperque paratis, In statione subatque expectantibus illam, Quo jubeat manare modo."
["A woman has always a fountain of tears ready to gush forth whenever she wishes to make use of them." — Juvenal, vi. 272.]

A man goes the wrong way to work when he opposes this passion; for opposition only irritates it and makes them more obstinate in their sorrow; the trouble is sharpened by argument. We see, in ordinary conversation, that something I have casually let drop, if anyone takes it up to contradict it, I defend with the best arguments I have — and far more so a thing in which I had a real interest. Besides, by doing so you enter roughly on your operation; whereas the first approach of a physician to his patient should be gracious, cheerful, and pleasing; never did any ill-looking, morose physician achieve anything. On the contrary, then, a man should at first favour their grief and show some approval of their sorrow. By this rapport you earn the credit to go further, and by an easy and imperceptible gradation fall into discourses more solid and more proper for their cure. I, whose main aim was to fool the company who had their eyes on me, took it into my head only to palliate the disease. And indeed I have found by experience that I have an unlucky hand at persuading. My arguments are either too sharp and dry, or pressed too roughly, or not driven home enough. After I had applied myself to her grief for some time, I did not attempt to cure her by strong and lively reasons, either because I had none at hand, or because I thought I could do my business better another way. Nor did I make use of any of the methods of consolation philosophy prescribes: that what we complain of is no evil, according to Cleanthes; that it is a slight evil, according to the Peripatetics; that to bemoan oneself is an action neither commendable nor just, according to Chrysippus; nor Epicurus's, more suited to my way, of shifting one's thoughts from afflicting things to pleasing ones; nor of bundling all these together to be used as the occasion calls, according to Cicero. But by gently bending my discourse, and digressing little by little, sometimes to subjects nearer, sometimes more remote from the purpose, as she gave me more or less attention, I imperceptibly led her away from that sorrowful thought, and kept her calm and in good humour while I stayed there. I made use of diversion. Those who came after me in the same service found no improvement in her, for I had not gone to the root.

I may, perhaps, have glanced elsewhere at some kind of public diversion. And the practice of military diversion, which Pericles used in the Peloponnesian war, and a thousand others in other places — to draw the enemy's forces out of their own country — is too common in history to need mention. It was an ingenious device by which Monseigneur d'Hempricourt saved both himself and others in the city of Liège, into which the Duke of Burgundy, who was besieging it, had made him enter to carry out the articles of their promised surrender. The people, assembled by night to deliberate on it, began to mutiny against the agreement, and several of them resolved to fall upon the commissioners, whom they had in their power. He, sensing the gusts of this first popular storm coming to break upon his lodgings, suddenly sent out to them two of the citizens (some of whom were with him) with new and milder terms to be proposed in their council, terms he had improvised then and there to meet his need. These two diverted the first tempest, carrying the enraged crowd back to the town hall to hear and consider what they had to say. The deliberation was short; a second storm arose as violent as the first. Whereupon he dispatched four new mediators of the same standing to meet them, protesting that he had now better conditions to present, ones that would entirely satisfy them; by this means the tumult was again calmed, and the people once more turned back to the council chamber. In short, by this dispensation of distractions, one after another, diverting their fury and dissipating it in frivolous consultations, he at last laid it to sleep until day broke — which was his principal aim.

This other story is of the same kind. Atalanta, a virgin of exceeding beauty and wonderful build of body, to disengage herself from the crowd of a thousand suitors who sought her hand, made this proposal: that she would accept as her husband whoever could equal her in running, on condition that those who failed should lose their lives. There were plenty who thought the prize well worth the risk, and who suffered the cruel penalty of the contract. Hippomenes, about to make his trial after the rest, addressed himself to the goddess of love, imploring her help; she, granting his request, gave him three golden apples, and instructed him how to use them. The race begun, as Hippomenes saw his mistress pressing hard upon him, he, as if by chance, let fall one of the apples; the maiden, taken with its beauty, did not fail to step out of her way to pick it up:
"Obstupuit Virgo, nitidique cupidine pomi Declinat cursus, aurumque volubile tollit."
["The virgin, astonished and drawn by the glittering apple, halts her course and seizes the rolling gold." — Ovid, Metam., x. 666.]

He did the same when he saw his chance with the second and the third, until by so diverting her, and making her lose so much ground, he won the race. When physicians cannot stop a catarrh, they divert and turn it into some other less dangerous part. And I find this is also the most ordinary practice for the diseases of the mind:
"Abducendus etiam nonnunquam animus est ad alia studia, sollicitudines, curas, negotia: loci denique mutatione, tanquam aegroti non convalescentes, saepe curandus est."

["The mind must sometimes be drawn off to other studies, thoughts, cares, business; and finally cured by change of place, as sick persons who are not recovering must be." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 35.]
It is to little effect to directly jostle a man's infirmities; we don't make him bear the attack, nor repel it; we only make him decline and evade it.

This other lesson is too high and too difficult: it is for men in the first rank of knowledge to insist purely on the thing, to consider and judge it; it belongs to only one Socrates to meet death with an ordinary countenance, to grow acquainted with it and to sport with it. He seeks no consolation from outside the thing itself; dying appears to him a natural and indifferent accident; it is there that he fixes his sight and his resolution, without looking elsewhere. The disciples of Hegesias, who starved themselves to death — drawn to it by his fine lectures, and in such numbers that King Ptolemy ordered him forbidden to entertain his followers with such homicidal doctrines — did not consider death in itself, nor judge of it; that is not where they fixed their thoughts; they were running toward and aiming at a new state of being.

The poor wretches we see brought to the scaffold, full of ardent devotion, and in it, as much as they can, employing all their senses — their ears in hearing the instructions given them, their eyes and hands lifted toward heaven, their voices in loud prayers, with a vehement and continual emotion — do, no doubt, things very commendable and proper for such a need; we must commend them for their devotion, but not properly for their constancy: they shun the encounter, they divert their thoughts from the consideration of death, as children are diverted with some toy when the surgeon is about to prick them with his lancet. I have seen some who, casting their eyes on the dreadful instruments of death set out around them, have fainted, and furiously turned their thoughts another way. Those who are to pass over a fearful precipice are advised either to shut their eyes or look another way.

Subrius Flavus, being ordered by Nero's command to be put to death by the hand of Niger, both of them great captains, when they led him to the place appointed for his execution, seeing the grave that Niger had had hollowed for him to be put into ill-made, said, turning to the soldiers who guarded him, "This is not even according to military discipline." And to Niger, who exhorted him to keep his head firm: "Just strike as firmly," he said. And he saw very well what would follow when he said so; for Niger's arm trembled so that he had to strike several blows at his head before he could cut it off. This man seems to have had his thoughts rightly fixed on his subject.

He who dies in battle, with his sword in his hand, does not then think about death; he feels it and considers it not; the ardour of the fight diverts his thought another way. A worthy man of my acquaintance, falling as he was fighting a duel and feeling himself nailed to the earth by nine or ten thrusts from his enemy, was urged on all sides to think of his conscience; but he later told me that, though he heard well enough what they said, it didn't move him at all, and that he thought of nothing but how to disengage and take his revenge. He afterwards killed his man in that very duel. He who brought to L. Silanus the sentence of death did him a very great kindness: for, having received Silanus's answer that he was well prepared to die but not by base hands, he ran upon him with his soldiers to force him; and as Silanus, unarmed as he was, obstinately defended himself with his fists and feet, the messenger made him lose his life in the struggle — in doing so dispelling and diverting, in a sudden and furious rage, the painful apprehension of the lingering death he had been designed for.

We always think of something else; either the hope of a better life comforts and supports us, or the hope of our children's worth, or the future glory of our name, or the leaving behind of this life's evils, or the vengeance that threatens those who are the cause of our death — these console us:
"Spero equidem mediis, si quid pia numina possunt, Supplicia hausurum scopulis, et nomine Dido Saepe vocaturum . . . . Audiam; et haec Manes veniet mihi fama sub imos."

["I hope, however, if the pious gods have any power, you will drink your punishment among the rocks, and will call on the name of Dido; I shall hear, and this report will come to me below." — Aeneid, iv. 382, 387.]

Xenophon was sacrificing, with a crown on his head, when someone came to tell him of the death of his son Gryllus, killed in the battle of Mantinea: at the first shock of the news, he threw his crown to the ground; but, learning from the rest of the report the manner of so brave and valiant a death, he picked it up again and put it back on his head. Epicurus himself, at his death, consoles himself with the usefulness and eternity of his writings:
"Omnes clari et nobilitati labores fiunt tolerabiles;"
["All labours that are illustrious and famous become bearable." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 26.]

— and the same wound, the same fatigue, is not, says Xenophon, so intolerable to a general of an army as to a common soldier. Epaminondas took his death much more cheerfully when he had been told that the victory remained with him:
"Haec sunt solatia, haec fomenta summorum dolorum;"
["These are the sedatives and salves of the greatest pains." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 23.]

— and such circumstances divert, amuse, and turn our thoughts from the consideration of the thing in itself. Even the arguments of philosophy are always edging and glancing along the matter, scarcely rubbing its crust. The greatest man of the first philosophical school, and superintendent over all the rest, the great Zeno, frames this syllogism against death: "No evil is honourable; but death is honourable; therefore death is no evil." Against drunkenness this: "No one entrusts his secrets to a drunkard; but everyone entrusts his secrets to a wise man; therefore a wise man is no drunkard." Is this hitting the bull's-eye? I love seeing that these great and leading souls cannot rid themselves of our company: perfect as they are, they are still simply men.

Revenge is a sweet passion, of great and natural impression; I see that well enough, though I have no experience of it. Not long ago, to divert a young prince from it, I did not tell him he must, to one who had struck him on the one cheek, turn the other, for the sake of charity; nor did I set out to represent for him the tragic events poetry attributes to that passion. I left that aside; and I busied myself making him relish the beauty of a contrary picture: representing to him what honour, esteem, and goodwill he would gain by clemency and good nature, I diverted him to ambition. That is how a man is to deal in such cases.

If your passion of love is too violent, disperse it, they say — and they speak truly, for I have often tried it with good results: break it into several desires, and let one be regent over the rest if you like; but, lest it tyrannize and lord it over you, weaken and dilute it by dividing and diverting it:
"Cum morosa vago singultiet inguine vena,"
["When you are tormented with fierce desire, satisfy it with the first person who presents herself." — Persius, Sat., vi. 73.]
"Conjicito humorem collectum in corpora quaeque,"
[Lucretius, vi. 1062, to the same effect.]
— and take care of it in time, lest it become troublesome to deal with once it has seized you:
"Si non prima novis conturbes vulnera plagis, Volgivagaque vagus venere ante recentia cures."
["Unless you cure old wounds with new." — Lucretius, iv. 1064.]

I was once wounded with a violent displeasure, and one more justified than violent; I might perhaps have lost myself in it had I trusted to my own strength alone. Needing a powerful diversion to disengage me, by art and study I made myself fall in love, which my youth assisted; love relieved me and rescued me from the trouble friendship had got me into. It is the same with everything else: a violent fancy has seized me; I find it a quicker way to change it than to subdue it; I substitute, if not a contrary one, at least another, in its place. Variety always relieves, dissolves, and dissipates.

If I am not able to contend with it, I escape from it; and in avoiding it, I slip out of the way and double back; shifting place, business, and company, I lose myself in the crowd of other thoughts and fancies, where it loses my trace and I escape.

Nature proceeds in the same way, by the benefit of inconstancy; for time, which she has given us as the sovereign physician of our passions, works chiefly in this — that by supplying our imagination with other and new things, it loosens and dissolves the first apprehension, however strong. A wise man sees his friend dying at the end of twenty-five years little less than he did in the first year, and, according to Epicurus, not less at all; for he attributed no relief from afflictions either to their foresight or their antiquity. But so many other thoughts cross this one that it languishes and tires at last.

Alcibiades, to divert the run of common gossip, cut off the ears and tail of his beautiful dog and turned him out into the public place, so that, giving the people this occasion to prate about it, they would let his other actions alone. I have also seen, for this same purpose of diverting people's opinions and conjectures and shutting their mouths, some women conceal their real affections under feigned ones; but I have also seen some who in pretending have let themselves be truly caught, and have abandoned their original true affection for the feigned one. From whom I learned that those who find their affections well placed are fools to consent to this disguise, since the public and favourable reception is reserved for the pretended lover. One may consider him a fellow of very little address and less wit if he doesn't in the end put himself in your place, and put you in his: that is precisely to cut out and stitch up a shoe for another to slip on.

A small thing will turn and divert us, because a small thing holds us. We do not much consider subjects in the gross, or singly; it is little and superficial circumstances, or images, that strike us — the outward useless rinds peeling off from the subjects themselves:
"Folliculos ut nunc teretes aestate cicadae Linquunt."
["As we find the husks grasshoppers leave behind them in summer." — Lucretius, v. 801.]

Even Plutarch himself laments his daughter for the little apish tricks of her infancy. The memory of a parting, of a particular grace in some action, of a last recommendation, troubles us. The sight of Caesar's robe troubled all of Rome — more than his death had done. Even the sound of names ringing in our ears, as "my poor master," "my faithful friend," "alas, my dear father," or "my sweet daughter," afflict us. When these repetitions hurt me, and I look at it a little more closely, I find it is no more than a grammatical and verbal complaint; I am only wounded by the word and tone, just as the exclamations of preachers often work more on their audience than their reasons do, and as the pitiful eyes of a beast killed for our service do — without my weighing or going into the meantime the true and solid essence of my subject:
"His se stimulis dolor ipse lacessit."
["With these spurs, grief provokes itself." — Lucretius, ii. 42.]
These are the foundations of our mourning.

The obstinacy of my stone, particularly in the bladder, has sometimes thrown me into such long suppressions of urine, for three or four days together, and so close to death, that it would have been folly to hope to escape it — and it was rather much more to be wished for, considering the miseries I endured in those cruel fits. Oh, that good emperor, who had criminals tied up to die for want of urination, was a great master in the hangman's science! Finding myself in this condition, I considered by how many slight causes and objects imagination kept the regret of life alive in me; of what atoms the weight and difficulty of this dislodging was compounded in my soul; to how many idle and frivolous thoughts we give way in so great a matter; a dog, a horse, a book, a glass — every kind of thing was considered in my loss; to others, their ambitious hopes, their money, their knowledge — no less foolish considerations than mine, in my opinion. I look on death carelessly when I look on it in general, as the end of life. I rule over it in the gross; but in detail, it dominates me; the tears of a footman, the disposing of my clothes, the touch of a friendly hand, a common consolation, discourages and softens me. So too the complaints in tragedies stir our souls with grief; and the laments of Dido and Ariadne move even those who don't believe them, in Virgil and Catullus. It is the mark of an obstinate and obdurate nature to be unmoved by any feeling, as is reported as a marvel of Polemon; but then he did not even change countenance at the bite of a mad dog that tore away the calf of his leg; and no wisdom goes so far as to grasp, by judgment alone, so vivid and entire a cause of sorrow that it does not allow it to be increased by its presence, when eyes and ears get their share — parts that can only be moved by vain accidents.

Is it reasonable that the arts themselves should take advantage of our natural stupidity and weakness? An orator, says rhetoric, in the farce of his pleading shall be moved by the sound of his own voice and his feigned emotions, and shall let himself be imposed on by the passion he is representing; he will imprint in himself a true and real grief by means of the part he is playing, in order to transmit it to the judges, who are less affected than he is; just like those hired at funerals to assist in the ceremony of sorrow, who sell their tears and mourning by weight and measure: for although they perform in a borrowed manner, nevertheless, by habituating and setting their countenances in the occasion, it is most certain that they often are really affected with actual sorrow. I was, with several other friends of his, one of those who conveyed the body of Monsieur de Grammont to Soissons from the siege of La Fère, where he was killed; and I noticed that in every place we passed through, we filled the people we met with lamentations and tears purely by the solemn pomp of our convoy — for the dead man's name was not even known there. Quintilian reports having seen comedians so deeply engaged in a mourning part that they were still weeping in the dressing room, and that, having undertaken to stir up passion in another, they have so espoused it themselves as to be infected by it, not only to the point of tears, but with pallor and the bearing of men really overwhelmed with grief.

In a country near our mountains, the women play "Priest Martin," for as they enlarge the regret for the dead husband by the remembrance of his good and agreeable qualities, they also at the same time make a register of and publish his imperfections — as if to enter into some compromise with themselves, and divert themselves from compassion to disdain. With much better grace than we do, who, when we lose an acquaintance, strive to give him new and false praises, and make him quite another thing once we have lost sight of him than he appeared to us when we did see him — as if regret were an instructive thing, or as if tears, by washing our understanding, cleared it. For my part, I henceforth renounce all favourable testimonies people may give of me, not because I shall deserve them, but because I shall be dead.

Ask a man, "What interest do you have in this siege?" — "The interest of example," he will say, "and of common obedience to my prince: I claim no profit from it; and as for glory, I know how small a share can fall to a private man like me; I have here neither passion nor quarrel." And yet you shall see him the next day quite another man, chafing and red with fury, ranged in the line of battle for the assault; it is the glitter of so much steel, the fire and noise of our cannon and drums, that have infused this new rigidity and fury into his veins. A frivolous cause, you will say. How a cause? There needs none to stir up the mind; a mere whim, without body and without subject, will rule it and agitate it. Let me think about building castles in Spain — my imagination supplies me with conveniences and pleasures by which my soul is really tickled and pleased. How often do we torment our mind with anger or sorrow by such shadows, and engage ourselves in fantastic passions that damage both soul and body! What astonished, fleeting, confused grimaces this raving puts on our faces! what sallies and stirrings, both of limbs and voices, it inspires us with! Does it not seem that this individual man has visions in the middle of the crowd he is dealing with, or that some internal demon is persecuting him? Ask yourself where the object of this change is: is there anything besides ourselves in nature that emptiness sustains, that emptiness has power over? Cambyses, having dreamt that his brother would one day be king of Persia, put him to death — a beloved brother, in whom he had always confided. Aristodemus, king of the Messenians, killed himself out of a fancy of ill omen, from I don't know what howling of his dogs; and King Midas did as much on account of some foolish dream he had had. It is to price life at its just value, to abandon it for a dream. And yet hear the soul triumph over the miseries and weakness of the body, and over its being exposed to every attack and alteration: truly, it has reason to speak so!
"O prima infelix finger ti terra Prometheo! Ille parum cauti pectoris egit opus Corpora disponens, mentem non vidit in arte; Recta animi primum debuit esse via."

["O wretched clay, first fashioned by Prometheus! In his attempt, how little wisdom he showed! In framing bodies, he did not apply his art to forming the mind, which should have been his first care." — Propertius, iii. 5, 7.]
